Surface: infra

## Current State

`manifesto.md`'s Step 3 ("Present the Manifesto") mandates, for default `auto` mode: "render the FYI variant... show the same preview + policy-levers tables, but change the heading to `### Pipeline Config (auto)`, drop the approval call entirely, and close with a single line — `→ proceeding (no approval needed) · run with confirm to review/override`."

Across this session's two `/flow` runs, this required visible render never appeared as assistant text. Both times, the levers were computed and written directly to `config.yml` via `set-config.js`, and the pipeline proceeded straight to dispatching the build — skipping the mandated table entirely. (The later, separately-gated Multi-Spec/single-spec Review Console tables — a different, `confirm`-style render at end-of-run — DID appear correctly both times, showing the skip is specific to this one step.)

This caused no functional harm (the config was still written and read correctly downstream), but it means a user running an "auto" pipeline received zero visibility into which policy levers were actually in effect for either run — the entire point of the Manifesto being a bookend "FYI" stop.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Decide the enforcement mechanism: (a) a conformance test (in the vein of the existing skill-prose-conformance suite) that asserts an `auto`-mode `/flow` transcript contains the FYI table text, making a skip visible after the fact even if unpreventable in-band; or (b) have `set-config.js` itself print the rendered table as part of its own stdout when invoked for the Manifesto step, so the render is a mechanical side effect of the write rather than something the orchestrating model must remember to compose separately; or (c) both.
- [ ] Implement the chosen mechanism(s).

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A fresh `auto`-mode `/flow` run's own output (or a mechanical check against its transcript/logs) demonstrably includes the `### Pipeline Config (auto)` table and the `→ proceeding (no approval needed)` line — not merely a `config.yml` write with no visible render.
2. `npm test` passes.

## Technical Approach

Option (b) is the more structurally reliable fix — a prose instruction ("render this table") is exactly the kind of step an LLM orchestrator can silently skip under time/context pressure, which is precisely what happened twice in this session; moving the render into `set-config.js`'s own stdout makes it a mechanical side effect of the write call the orchestrator already makes, not a separate step to remember. Option (a) (a conformance test) can't prevent a live skip — a `node --test` suite only pins prose/fixture shape, it can't observe a real `/flow` session's actual transcript — so it's better understood as after-the-fact detection (useful for catching regressions in a fixture-driven test harness, if one exists for `/flow` runs) than a fix for the live-session problem this record's own evidence describes. Weigh both against `set-config.js`'s existing call sites (the batch write already documented in `manifesto.md`'s "Write mechanism" section) — adding a render to its stdout must not break any caller that doesn't expect extra output.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/flow/manifesto.md` — Step 3's FYI-variant render instruction (the mandate this record found unenforced) and the "Write mechanism" section describing `set-config.js`'s batch call
- `plugin/bin/set-config.js` — the CLI this record's fix likely extends to print the rendered table itself (Technical Approach option (b))

## Gotchas

- This is a two-run sample (both `/flow` invocations in one session skipped the render the same way) — real but small evidence; if the build phase wants stronger confirmation the skip is systemic rather than session-specific, a few more observed runs would strengthen the case, though the underlying "prose instructions are skippable" reasoning holds regardless of sample size.
- Don't let option (b)'s stdout addition break `set-config.js`'s non-Manifesto callers (the ceremony-escape single-key form, `steps-and-gates.md` case 3's recovery writes) — scope the new render to the Manifesto-specific batch call site, not every invocation of the CLI.

Surface: infra

## Current State

`/flow`'s worktree-creation step (`materialize.md`'s worktree-first ordering, `build/worktree-setup.md`) is documented to open the pipeline's draft PR early ("born public" — `_shared/pr-early-run-lifecycle.md`), before any build work happens. In this session's two `/flow` runs (spec-2670-2681, spec-2682), that PR was NOT created automatically at worktree-creation time — a bare `git` worktree was created and a build subagent dispatched directly. Both build subagents independently hit `build/worktree-setup.md`'s own pre-tool-use hook gate (`checkBookkeepingStampsGate`, per `docs/incident-log.md` `[IL-131]`) blocking further edits until a PR was recorded, and both had to improvise: run `record-worktree`/`record-pr` CLI commands and `gh pr create` themselves, mid-task, outside their own declared spec scope.

Session evidence:
- Spec #2670's build agent: "This run's PR-early lifecycle step (`build/worktree-setup.md` Step 6) had not run before I was dispatched — the `pre-tool-use` hook (IL-131) blocked all `Edit` calls until it was satisfied. I completed it: pushed the branch, opened draft PR #2698... This is infrastructure the orchestrating pipeline should normally have done at run start, not part of #2670's own deliverables."
- Spec #2682's build agent: "had to open this draft PR mid-task — the repo's `pr-first` hook blocked further edits until a PR was recorded; used `record-worktree` then `record-pr` CLI commands to satisfy the gate."

**Root cause, narrowed during shaping.** `build/SKILL.md`'s own text (Spec Step 1, ~line 68) already documents the draft-PR call as non-skippable: "Immediately after the materialize commit, in `worktree` mode only: run `build/worktree-setup.md` Step 6 — opens the run's draft PR under `integration-model: pr-first`... Non-skippable, regardless of what Spec Step 2's implementation assessment turns out to find." It also already carries a reactive backstop for exactly this failure mode: `build/SKILL.md`'s Common Step 7 "Bookkeeping assertion" (#2311) checks `run-state.json` for a missing `worktree`/`pr` field at the end of every build phase and backfills it — this is the mechanism [IL-131] traces to, and it's *already shipped*, not a gap this record needs to invent.

Critically, `build/worktree-setup.md` itself states Step 6 "is invoked separately from `build/SKILL.md` Spec Step 1, never from within this numbered procedure" — i.e. Common Step 1 (worktree creation) and Step 6 (open the draft PR) are two *separate* calls, and only `build/SKILL.md`'s own Spec Step 1 sequences them together. This session's `/flow` runs hand-rolled worktree creation (`EnterWorktree` + a bare `Agent` dispatch for "build") rather than literally invoking `/claude-tweaks:build` as a `Skill`-tool call — which means Spec Step 1's own explicit Step 6 call, and Common Step 7's own end-of-phase backfill, were both bypassed entirely, since neither lives in the hand-rolled path at all. A grep of `flow/SKILL.md` for "PR-early"/"draft PR" during this shaping pass returned zero matches — the requirement genuinely isn't stated in `flow/SKILL.md`'s own Step 4 prose at all, only in the two files `build/SKILL.md` cross-references.

This strongly supports root-cause (b) from the original report (a hand-rolled orchestration path, not a gap in `/flow`/`/build`'s own documented-and-enforced sequence) — but the fix still needs a decision on where to close the gap: strengthen `flow/SKILL.md`'s own Step 4 prose so an orchestrator following it by hand (not literally invoking the Skill tool) can't miss the requirement, and/or consider whether Common Step 1 itself should absorb the Step 6 call so the two can't be separated by construction.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Add explicit PR-early language to `flow/SKILL.md`'s Step 4 (currently silent on it — confirmed via grep during shaping) naming the requirement plainly enough that a hand-executing orchestrator (not literally invoking the `Skill` tool) won't miss it, cross-referencing `build/worktree-setup.md` Step 6 and `_shared/pr-early-run-lifecycle.md`.
- [ ] Evaluate whether `build/worktree-setup.md`'s Common Step 1 (worktree creation) should call Step 6 (open draft PR) directly, removing the separate-invocation fragility that let this session's hand-rolled path skip it — implement if the evaluation favors it; document the decision either way if not (e.g. if a real reason keeps them separate, such as a caller that legitimately needs the worktree before deciding whether a PR applies).
- [ ] Confirm `build/SKILL.md`'s existing Common Step 7 Bookkeeping-assertion backstop (#2311) still fires correctly for a *literal* `/claude-tweaks:build` invocation — this record's own investigation didn't find a gap there, only in the hand-rolled path that bypasses `build/SKILL.md` entirely; no changes needed there unless testing turns up a real gap.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A fresh `/flow #{n}` run (or `/build #{n}` standalone) opens its draft PR before the first implementer edit, with no build-time hook block requiring mid-task improvisation.
2. `flow/SKILL.md`'s Step 4 states the PR-early requirement explicitly — a reader following the prose by hand, without invoking the `Skill` tool literally, has enough information to not skip it.
3. `npm test` passes.

## Technical Approach

Two independent angles, both grounded in the investigation above: (1) a documentation fix to `flow/SKILL.md`'s Step 4, which currently says nothing about PR-early at all; (2) an architectural question about whether `worktree-setup.md`'s Common Step 1 and Step 6 should be coupled rather than two separately-invoked steps — resolve this by reading `build/SKILL.md`'s Spec Step 1 prose (~line 68) and `worktree-setup.md`'s own Step 6 comment about being invoked separately, then deciding whether coupling them removes real flexibility (some caller legitimately needing worktree-without-PR) or is pure accidental fragility.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/flow/SKILL.md` — Step 4, where the PR-early requirement needs stating explicitly
- `plugin/skills/build/SKILL.md` — Spec Step 1 (~line 68, the existing non-skippable PR-early call) and Common Step 7 (the #2311 Bookkeeping-assertion backstop)
- `plugin/skills/build/worktree-setup.md` — Common Step 1 (worktree creation) and Step 6 (draft PR open), and its own comment on why they're currently separate calls
- `plugin/skills/_shared/pr-early-run-lifecycle.md` — the push-and-open-draft-PR procedure both Step 6 and the Bookkeeping-assertion backfill call

## Gotchas

- Don't conclude the reactive backstop (#2311's Bookkeeping assertion) is broken — this investigation found no evidence of that; the gap is specific to a hand-rolled orchestration path that bypasses `build/SKILL.md` (and therefore both the Step 6 call and the Common Step 7 backstop) entirely, not a failure of `/claude-tweaks:build`'s own documented sequence when actually invoked.
- If coupling Common Step 1 and Step 6 turns out to have a legitimate reason to stay separate (check for one before assuming there isn't), the fix narrows to the documentation angle alone — don't force a code change the investigation doesn't support.

`_shared/worktree-setup.md`'s "Post-creation catch-up" section states: "When either merge actually advances the worktree's branch ... the calling procedure appends an entry to the run's `decisions.md` under its own heading." This assumes a pipeline run directory (and its `decisions.md`) already exists at the point the catch-up merge runs. Notably, this repo's own CLAUDE.md already practices a related discipline manually — its `## Don'ts` section states "Full rule list now lives in docs/donts.md (moved out of this always-loaded file to fit the 150-line budget)" — so a lint/audit check would formalize and enforce a budget this repo already tries to hold ad hoc.

- Running the check against a sample of enrolled repos' CLAUDE.md files reports a pass/fail against the line-count guidance.

Add a mechanical line-count + largest-section-size check, following the existing pattern of a `/code-health` or `harness-health` scan step (a metadata-only read: file path, line count, section boundaries via `##`/`###` heading scan — never reading full section prose into a report unless flagging it). `skills/simplify/SKILL.md`'s Step 2 names the completion-notification requirement (or an equivalent wait primitive) as a precondition for the diff-and-revert check, so a caller following the instructions as written cannot repeat this race.

## Current State
Deleting a user from the production database on account deletion leaves their personal data intact in rolling database backups (e.g. a 30-day retention window), which can violate GDPR right-to-erasure. Rewriting, decrypting, and recompressing terabytes of backup data to scrub one user on every deletion request is operationally expensive and can overwhelm production systems. Cryptographic erasure — encrypting each user's sensitive data with a unique per-user key and destroying only that key on deletion — makes the backup copy unreadable without ever touching the backup itself. 2. Document the cryptographic-erasure pattern (per-user key encryption + key destruction on deletion) as the recommended fix when a project keeps rolling backups containing user PII.
3. Ship a copy-paste prompt, matching this pipeline's existing pattern for this class of check, that walks a codebase through checking for this specific gap.

Surface: infra

## Current State
`checkOneFixture` in `tools/upstream-drift/checks.js` (lines 330-380) replays a manifest fixture command and asserts its observed output against `expect`. The function hard-requires the named stream (`expect.stream`, `stdout` or `stderr`) to parse as JSON — `tryParseJson(streams[wanted].trim())` — and returns a mismatch if it doesn't, including a special case that names when the JSON payload landed on the other stream instead. This makes it impossible to write a fixture for a command whose failure output is plain text rather than JSON. This was discovered while auditing #2480 (Impeccable CLI Rust-engine shim): the engine-locate/download failure path writes a plain-text message to stderr and exits 127, but there is no way to assert that exact behavior as a fixture today — only a JSON-shaped stderr/stdout payload is expressible.

## Deliverables
1. Extend `checkOneFixture` to support a plain-text/substring assertion mode on a named stream, as an alternative to the existing JSON-parse assertion — expressible via a new `expect` field (e.g. `expect.contains` or `expect.textMatch`) that, when present, asserts a substring match on `streams[expect.stream]` instead of requiring JSON parse.
2. Update the manifest schema/validation (`tools/upstream-drift/manifest.js`) to accept the new field alongside the existing `exit`/`stream`/`keys` fields, validating that a fixture specifies either the JSON-mode fields or the new text-mode field, not an ambiguous mix.
3. Add a fixture to `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml` (or a test-only manifest) exercising the plain-text stderr case from #2480 (or an equivalent), to prove the new mode round-trips a real plain-text failure.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. A fixture whose `expect` includes the new text-mode field and a substring that appears in the named stream's actual output passes `checkOneFixture`.
2. A fixture whose `expect` includes the new text-mode field and a substring that does NOT appear in the named stream's actual output returns a `mismatch` result with a detail naming the expected substring and which stream was checked.
3. Existing JSON-mode fixtures (using `expect.keys`) are unaffected — `checkOneFixture`'s existing JSON-parse path and its stdout/stderr swap detection continue to work exactly as before for fixtures that don't use the new field.
4. The manifest validation in `manifest.js` accepts fixtures using the new text-mode field without requiring the JSON-mode `keys` field, and still validates `exit`/`stream` are present as it does today.
5. A fixture reproducing the #2480 plain-text-stderr/exit-127 case round-trips correctly (passes when the actual behavior matches, fails with an informative detail when it regresses).

## Technical Approach
Add a new optional `expect` field for text/substring assertion, checked in `checkOneFixture` before or alongside the existing JSON-parse branch: if the text-mode field is present, skip the JSON-parse requirement entirely and instead check `streams[wanted].includes(expectedSubstring)`, returning a `mismatch` with a clear detail (naming the expected substring and observed stream) on failure. Keep the existing JSON-parse path unchanged for fixtures that don't opt into the new field — the two modes should be mutually exclusive per fixture, decided by which `expect` fields are present. Update `manifest.js`'s fixture validation to allow this new field and to require that a fixture uses exactly one assertion mode (JSON-mode via `keys`, or text-mode via the new field) rather than allowing both or neither silently.

### Key Files
- `tools/upstream-drift/checks.js` — `checkOneFixture` (lines 330-380): add the text/substring assertion branch, keep the JSON-parse path unchanged for non-opted-in fixtures
- `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.js` — fixture schema validation: accept the new `expect` field, enforce mutually-exclusive assertion mode
- `tools/upstream-drift/manifest.yml` — add or extend a fixture exercising the plain-text-stderr case from #2480
- `tools/upstream-drift/tests/manifest.test.js` — add test coverage for the new field's validation
- `tools/upstream-drift/tests/checks.test.js` (if it exists; otherwise the relevant checks test file) — add test coverage for the new text-mode assertion branch in `checkOneFixture`

## Gotchas
The two assertion modes (JSON-parse vs. text/substring) must stay mutually exclusive per fixture — allowing both to be specified together would create ambiguous validation semantics. The existing stdout/stderr-swap detection in the JSON-parse path is a load-bearing anti-regression check (comment at checks.js:361-366 calls it "the single most important case this function exists to catch"); the new text-mode path does not need to replicate that specific swap-detection logic unless a plain-text payload swap becomes a realized failure mode worth catching, but should not regress the existing JSON-mode swap detection.

## Original request

upstream-drift checkOneFixture cannot assert plain-text stderr, only JSON

**Related:** #2480

Context: Discovered auditing #2480 (Impeccable CLI Rust-engine shim) -- the engine-locate/download failure writes a plain-text message to stderr and exits 127, but checkOneFixture (tools/upstream-drift/checks.js:359-369) hard-requires the asserted stream to parse as JSON.

Scope: Extend checkOneFixture (or add a sibling assertion mode) to support a text/substring match on a named stream, so a plain-text failure like this becomes expressible as a fixture.

Surface: infra

## Current State
Two recurring coding-agent anti-patterns have been identified from an external source (a transcribed Instagram Reel from a developer who has shipped 15+ AI-built apps):

1. **Polling instead of realtime push** — agents building a data flow that needs live updates default to fixed-interval polling (e.g. `setInterval` fetches every few seconds) instead of a realtime push/subscription mechanism when the backend already supports one (e.g. a Supabase/Convex subscription, a websocket, SSE). This looks fine in testing but drains battery and degrades frame rate under real usage.
2. **Duplicate "v2" files instead of in-place edits** — agents avoid replacing working code in place, instead layering a `v2`/duplicate-suffixed file or function on top "just in case." This leaves dead code around, and the agent loses track of which version is actually live, leading to circular, self-breaking edits on later requests.

Anti-pattern 2 is already a standing instruction in this repo's own CLAUDE.md ("don't use feature flags or backwards-compatibility shims when you can just change the code" — see the Philosophy/Don'ts sections) — the external source is independent confirmation that the same failure mode is common enough across coding agents generally to be worth a dedicated automated review check, not just a written instruction the agent might drift from under pressure.

Neither anti-pattern currently has an automated review-lens check.

## Deliverables
1. Add a review-lens check that flags a newly introduced fixed-interval polling loop (`setInterval`/`setTimeout` recursion, or an equivalent polling construct) against a data source that already exposes or could reasonably expose a realtime push/subscription mechanism.
2. Add a review-lens check that flags a newly created file or function with a version-suffix name pattern (`v2`, `-new`, `-copy`, `_updated`, etc.) sitting alongside an unremoved original that the diff did not delete or fully migrate away from.
3. Document that these two checks formalize the existing CLAUDE.md "change code in place" instruction into an automated check, rather than relying on the instruction alone.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The polling check flags a sample diff that adds a fixed-interval polling loop against a realtime-capable backend.
- The polling check does not flag polling against a data source with no realtime alternative available (e.g. a third-party REST API with no push option).
- The duplicate-version check flags a sample diff that introduces a `v2`-suffixed (or equivalent) file/function alongside its unremoved original.
- The duplicate-version check does not flag a legitimate versioned artifact (e.g. an API route intentionally versioned as `/v2/` for external consumers) — the check targets abandoned/duplicated internal code, not a deliberate external contract.
- Documentation for the review-lens (or the relevant skill's checklist) states that these two checks formalize the existing CLAUDE.md instruction into an automated check.

## Technical Approach
Locate where existing review-lens checks live (likely under `/claude-tweaks:review`'s checks or a related lens-definition file) and read at least one existing check to match its structure and severity/reporting conventions. Add the two new checks following that same structure, including copy-paste-able flag conditions and a false-positive guard for each (realtime-unavailable backends for the polling check; deliberately-versioned external contracts for the duplicate-version check).

No check for a journey's peak/end moments (Peak-End Rule), spatial grouping of related controls (Proximity), or a single visually distinct emphasis element (Von Restorff Effect).

- Cite the law by name in the check's explanation so violations are self-documenting.

## Acceptance Criteria
